title: Parents visiting the UK fall ill: GPs, A&E, NHS charges and insurance
summary: How parents visiting England on a visitor visa can see a GP, use A&E and 111, which hospital treatment is charged at 150%, and how insurance, medicines, interpreters and unpaid bills affect them.
content:
# Parents visiting the UK fall ill: GPs, A&E, NHS charges and insurance

Last updated: 2026-11-27

> This guide covers **England**. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have different rules on healthcare and charges for visitors, and we will cover them separately.

When parents come for a rare visit and stay for several months, what families worry about most is often not food or accommodation, but what happens if they fall ill during the stay.

First, the overall picture: in England, visiting parents can see a GP and can go to A&E. But "can be seen" and "free" are two different things. A GP consultation and A&E itself are generally free, but follow-on hospital treatment, such as being admitted or returning for follow-up appointments, is charged to visitors unless an exemption applies.

## Your IHS does not cover your parents

It is best to understand this from the start. The IHS you paid with your visa lets you use the NHS like a long-term resident while your visa is valid. It does not extend to parents who come to visit.

Your parents are on a visitor visa, do not pay the IHS, and so do not get the entitlements that come with it. Their healthcare in the UK follows the rules for "overseas visitors". Everything below is about those rules. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ihs-does-not-cover-visiting-parents)

## Minor illnesses: they can see a GP

In England, anyone can register with and see a GP, and consultations are free, including for visitors. Registration does not require an NHS number, and there is no rule that you must have lived in the UK for a certain time first. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-gp-free-for-any-visitor)

If they will stay near your home for a while — more than 24 hours but less than 3 months — they can apply for temporary registration with a GP practice there. NHS England's guidance to practices is that people living in the practice area for that length of time should be offered the option of temporary registration. You can phone or visit the practice, explain to reception that these are parents visiting family, and ask to register them temporarily. The exact process may vary between practices; a practice can refuse, but it needs a reasonable reason. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-temporary-registration-for-visitors)

Even if they cannot register, if a doctor judges that something needs dealing with straight away, the GP practice has a duty to provide emergency or immediately necessary treatment, regardless of nationality or immigration status; under NHS England guidance, the practice must then also provide 14 days of further cover. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-gp-immediately-necessary-treatment)

Registering with a GP only means they can be seen at that practice; it does not mean hospital care will be free. When a GP refers a patient to hospital, the hospital decides separately whether charges apply. These are two separate things. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-gp-registration-separate-from-hospital-charges)

Also, a free GP consultation does not mean everything that follows is free. The NHS website says visitors usually have to pay for prescriptions, dental treatment and eye tests themselves. Prescriptions in England cost £9.90 per item. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-visitors-pay-prescriptions-dental-eye-tests)

## Emergencies: A&E and 999

For a serious injury or a life-threatening emergency, go straight to A&E. No appointment is needed, and they do not need an NHS number or to be registered with a GP first. Under England's charging rules for visitors, emergency services in A&E are free, as long as the person did not come to the UK specifically to get treatment. The same applies to emergency services at walk-in centres, minor injuries units and urgent care centres. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-ae-free-unless-travelled-for-treatment)

If it may be life-threatening, call 999 straight away. The same rules state that emergency ambulances are also a free emergency service, on the same condition: the person did not come to the UK to get treatment. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-call-999-and-emergency-ambulance)

Worries about payment or immigration status should never be a reason to delay calling 999 or going to A&E. The rule in England is that treatment a doctor judges to be urgent or immediately necessary must never be delayed or refused because of charges, even if the patient cannot or will not pay. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-urgent-care-never-withheld)

If you are not sure whether to go to A&E, call 111 or ask at 111.nhs.uk first. Calling 111 is itself free. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-111-when-unsure)

## If they need to be admitted after A&E, things change

This is the part you most need to be clear about.

"A&E is free" refers to care in A&E itself. If the doctor decides your parent should be admitted to hospital (formally becoming an inpatient), or come back for follow-up outpatient appointments, this is no longer free emergency care and is charged unless an exemption applies. Visitors who have to pay are charged 150% of the cost of NHS treatment (100% for a small number of people covered by specific agreements). [See the official source](#guide-evidence-inpatient-and-follow-up-charges)

A few points here are easily confused:

- **treatment a doctor judges to be urgent or immediately necessary is given first**, and will not be delayed because of money; [See the official source](#guide-evidence-urgent-care-never-withheld)
- **but being treated first does not make it free**. If it is not exempt, the hospital will still send a bill after the treatment;
- **if the doctor judges that the treatment is not urgent**, the rule is pay first, then treatment; without payment, the hospital is not allowed to provide this kind of non-urgent treatment. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-non-urgent-treatment-paid-in-advance)

The doctor may also first stabilise the patient so they can be safely discharged and return home for further treatment, to avoid running up more costs in the UK. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-stabilise-and-return-home)

Some things are free, such as diagnosing and treating certain infectious diseases; each exemption has its own conditions. Hospitals have staff who deal specifically with charges for visitors (overseas visitor managers) and decide whether charges apply; during this process they may ask about status and visas. If charges do apply, the hospital should give you a written statement explaining why, the estimated cost and how to pay. If you have questions, ask them directly. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-other-exemptions-and-written-charge-statement)

## Why insurance matters

The NHS advice is clear: visitors should have personal medical or travel insurance covering the whole of their stay in the UK. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-visitor-insurance-whole-visit)

The reason is explained above: GP and A&E care are generally free, but once someone is admitted to hospital, the costs can be high, and visitors usually have to pay them.

What a policy covers, how to claim, whether existing long-term conditions are included, and whether the policy covers the trip to the UK all depend on the policy wording, and policies vary a lot. It is best to read the policy carefully before travelling and ask the insurer directly if you have questions. We do not go into these details here.

## Regular medicines

Many older people take medicine every day. Before coming, it is best to bring enough, and write down the medicine names and doses, ideally with the generic name (the name of the active ingredient). UK prescribing generally uses the generic name, and a brand name used abroad may be unfamiliar here.

If any of the medicines contain controlled drugs, the rules are stricter: they can only bring up to 3 months' supply, and anything more will be seized (a personal licence can be applied for in advance in special cases); they must also carry a letter proving the medicine was prescribed for them, with their name, travel dates, the medicines and doses, signed by the prescriber. For ordinary medicines that are not controlled drugs, we have not found any official overall limit on quantity, so we do not give a specific number here; it is safest to bring what is actually needed, in the original packaging. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-controlled-drugs-for-visitors)

If medicine is running low, it is best to contact the GP they are temporarily registered with in good time, or ask 111 what to do, rather than waiting until it runs out completely. Pharmacies in England can sometimes supply certain emergency medicines without a prescription, but you may have to pay. Whether something can be supplied, and what, is for a UK doctor or pharmacist to decide. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-running-out-of-medicine)

## What if they don't speak English?

At a GP practice, they can ask for an interpreter when booking an appointment and say which language they need. Under NHS England guidance, interpreting should be provided free, and the practice should not charge patients or ask them to bring their own interpreter. You can also ask for an interpreter when calling 111. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-gp-interpreter-free)

NHS England's guidance discourages relying on family or friends to interpret, and children under 16 should not interpret at all except in an emergency. So however good the grandchildren's English is, it is best not to have them interpret in the consulting room. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-family-and-child-interpreters)

For hospitals, Healthwatch (the statutory body that represents patients' views in England) says patients can ask for a professional interpreter at every stage of their care and should not have to pay for it; however, each hospital has its own arrangements. Tell the hospital what language or dialect is needed and ask about its interpreting arrangements. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-hospital-interpreter)

## What happens if a bill is not paid?

This is worth knowing, but it should not make anyone afraid to get care.

Hospital bills are normally the responsibility of the patient who received the treatment. If a bill remains unpaid, the debt is more than £500, more than two months have passed since the invoice and there is no agreement to pay by instalments, the hospital must report the debt; it is passed through the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) to the Home Office, and the patient should be told that the debt has been reported. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-debt-reporting)

Under the current UK Immigration Rules (SUI 16.1 in Part Suitability), if unpaid NHS charges of this kind reach £500, a future UK visa application may be refused because of them. This is "may", not "will": the Home Office's guidance for caseworkers says they must not refuse automatically and must look at the circumstances. Written confirmation from the hospital that the debt has been paid, or that an instalment plan has been agreed and is being kept to, will be taken into account. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-debt-discretionary-refusal)

So if you receive a bill and cannot pay it straight away, contacting the hospital to agree instalments is much better than ignoring it — debts with an agreed instalment plan are not reported in the first place. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-nhs-debt-reporting)

## What to prepare before your parents come

- The generic name, dose and instructions for each medicine, ideally in English;
- allergies, and their main medical history and current treatment;
- the insurance policy, the insurer's contact details and emergency contact details;
- the name and phone number of a GP practice near your home, and whether they should apply for temporary registration;
- a few numbers to remember: call 999 if someone's life is at risk, and 111 if you are not sure (or go to 111.nhs.uk).
